title: A Scientist Working on the ‘IceCube’ Neutrino Detector Explains the Nobel Prize–Winning Technology
gist: Juan Carlos Diaz Velez of the IceCube collaboration explains the work behind Francis Halzen's 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics: a 1 cubic kilometer array of 5,160 sensors in South Pole ice that detects high-energy cosmic neutrinos. The project, a 450-person international collaboration, traced neutrinos to a blazar and the Milky Way, and relies on about 10,000 CPU cores and 1,000 GPUs.

insights.claim: IceCube uses 5,160 optical sensors buried across 1 cubic kilometer of very transparent South Pole ice at 1.5 kilometers depth to detect light from muons produced in rare neutrino-ice interactions.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of infrastructure behind frontier astrophysics.
insights.locator: And the team Díaz Vélez is part of

insights.claim: Detecting a neutrino is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: for every neutrino IceCube detects, over a million muons from cosmic rays are detected.
insights.speaker: Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez
insights.so_what: Signal-to-noise filtering is the central data challenge.
insights.quote: For every neutrino IceCube detects, more than a million muons produced by cosmic rays are detected.
insights.locator: Cosmic rays consist of protons and nuclei

insights.claim: High-energy neutrinos are perfect messengers from cosmic-ray sources because they travel straight and unaffected by magnetic fields, with the highest-energy detected sources being active galactic nuclei with supermassive black holes.
insights.speaker: Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez
insights.so_what: Opens a new channel for astronomy alongside light and gamma rays.
insights.quote: That is why neutrinos are perfect messengers from high-energy cosmic-ray sources.
insights.locator: When these particles collide with the interstellar medium

insights.claim: IceCube's first major discovery was neutrinos from astrophysical sources outside the solar system, notably blazar TXS 0506+056, and it has since observed the Milky Way as a diffuse neutrino source.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Confirms blazars as neutrino sources and establishes neutrino astronomy.

insights.claim: Cosmic rays arrive from preferred directions rather than uniformly, which tells scientists about the distribution of their sources in the galaxy.
insights.speaker: Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez
insights.so_what: Adds a constraint for models of galactic cosmic-ray sources.
insights.locator: Another area of research is cosmic rays

insights.claim: IceCube processing computes direction, energy and particle type every two milliseconds and requires simulations at comparable rates on distributed networks of roughly 10,000 CPU cores and 1,000 GPUs.
insights.speaker: Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez
insights.so_what: Illustrates substantial distributed compute demand in big-science projects.
insights.locator: Díaz Vélez serves as the product coordinator

insights.claim: IceCube is an international collaboration of 450 people at 58 institutions across 14 countries, with many students, so the Nobel recognizes the work of dozens of colleagues behind one name.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Shows how large collaborations underlie single-name prizes.

insights.claim: Díaz Vélez says Halzen's passion and dedication made the experiment succeed, and the team sees him more as a colleague than a boss.

insights.so_what: Leadership credited as key to long-horizon science.
